**Tafsir (exegesis) of Surah al-Fil.** It is Meccan by scholarly consensus. It has five verses.

In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful.

In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful.

﴿Have you not considered how your Lord dealt with the companions of the elephant?﴾ (105:1)

There are five issues here.

**The first issue:** His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿أَلَمْ تَرَ﴾ ("Have you not seen"), means: "Have you not been informed?" It is also said to mean: "Do you not know?" Ibn 'Abbas said: "Have you not heard?" The wording is a question, but the meaning is an affirmation. The address is to the Prophet ﷺ, but it is general in meaning, as if to say: "Have you not seen what I did to the companions of the elephant?" That is, you have indeed seen it, and you know the place of My favour upon you. So why do you not believe? The word ﴿كَيْفَ﴾ ("how") is in the accusative position, governed by ﴿فَعَلَ﴾ ("did"), not by ﴿أَلَمْ تَرَ﴾. Within the sense of a question, ﴿كَيْفَ﴾ is only an interrogative.

**The second issue:** His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿بِأَصْحَابِ الْفِيلِ﴾ ("the companions of the elephant"). The *fil* (elephant) is well known. Its plurals are *afyal*, *fuyul* and *fiyala*. Ibn al-Sikkit said: "Do not say *afila*." The female is *fila*, and its keeper is *fayyal*. Sibawayh said: "It is possible that the original form of *fil* was *fu'l*, and it was given a kasra because of the *ya'*, as they said *abyad* and *bid*." Al-Akhfash said: "This does not occur in the singular; it occurs only in the plural." A man described as *fil al-ra'y* means one of weak opinion, whose plural is *afyal*. A man described as *fall* means one of weak opinion who errs in discernment. The opinion *fal* (became weak), *yafil*, *fuyula*. He *fayyala* his opinion, *tafyilan*, meaning he weakened it. So he is *fayyil al-ra'y*.

**The third issue:** Concerning the story of the companions of the elephant: Abraha built the Qullays in Sana'a. It was a church (*kanisa*) such that none like it had been seen in its time anywhere on earth. He was a Christian. Then he wrote to the Negus: "I have built for you, O king, a church the like of which was never built for any king before you, and I shall not desist until I divert to it the pilgrimage of the Arabs." When the Arabs spoke of Abraha's letter to the Negus, a man from the *Nasa'a* [in the Sira of Ibn Hisham: "a man from the Nasa'a, one of Banu Fuqaym ibn 'Adi..." The *Nasa'a* were those who postponed the sacred months for the Arabs in the Jahiliyya, making a sacred month lawful and making in its place a month that was not sacred, and delaying that month. Concerning this Allah, Blessed and Exalted, revealed: ﴿إِنَّمَا النَّسِيءُ زِيَادَةٌ فِي الْكُفْرِ﴾ ("The postponement is only an increase in disbelief") (9:37). See the Sira of Ibn Hisham, European edition, p.] became angry. He went out until he came to the church and sat in it, that is, he defecated in it, then he left and returned to his land. Abraha was informed of this and said: "Who did this?" It was said: "A man from the people of this House, the one to which the Arabs make pilgrimage in Mecca. When he heard your saying, 'I shall divert to it the pilgrimage of the Arabs,' he became angry, so he came and sat in it," meaning that it was not worthy of that. At that, Abraha became furious and swore that he would march upon the House and demolish it. He sent a man he had with him to the Banu Kinana [Banu Kinana: the tribe of that man who defiled the church] calling them to make pilgrimage to that church. The Banu Kinana killed that man, and this increased Abraha's anger and rage. Then he ordered the Abyssinians, and they prepared and equipped themselves. He set out, and the elephant went with him. The Arabs heard of this, they considered it grave and were horrified by it, and they regarded his fighting as a duty upon them, when they heard that he intended to demolish the Ka'ba, the Sacred House of Allah. A man of the nobles and kings of Yemen, called Dhu Nafr, went out against him. He called his people and those of the rest of the Arabs who answered him to fight Abraha and to defend the Sacred House of Allah against what he intended to demolish and destroy. Those who answered him did so. Then he confronted him and fought him, and Dhu Nafr and his companions were defeated. Dhu Nafr was taken captive and brought before him. When he wanted to kill him, Dhu Nafr said: "O king, do not kill me, for perhaps my remaining with you may be better for you than my death." So he spared him from being killed and kept him bound in his custody. Abraha was a forbearing man. Then Abraha went on in that direction, seeking what he had set out for, until when he was in the land of Khath'am, Nufayl ibn Habib al-Khath'ami met him, with the two Khath'am tribes, Shahran and Nahis, and those of the Arab tribes who followed him. He fought him and Abraha defeated him, and Nufayl was taken captive and brought. When he wanted to kill him, Nufayl said: "O king, do not kill me, for I am your guide in the land of the Arabs, and these are my hands given to you over the two tribes of Khath'am, Shahran and Nahis, with obedience and submission." So he released him, and he went with him guiding him. When he passed by al-Ta'if, Mas'ud ibn Mu'attib went out to him with men of Thaqif and said to him: "O king, we are only your servants, obedient and listening to you; we have no opposition to you. This house [they meant al-Lat, the idol in al-Ta'if, the house they used to venerate much as the Ka'ba is venerated] is not the one you seek. You seek only the house in Mecca. We will send with you one who will guide you to it." So he left them alone. They sent with him Abu Righal, and he brought him down at al-Mughammas [al-Mughammas: a place near Mecca on the road to al-Ta'if]. When he settled him there, Abu Righal died there. The Arabs stoned his grave, and it is the grave that people stone at al-Mughammas. Concerning this the poet says:

*And I stone his grave every year,*
*as people stone the grave of Abu Righal.*

When Abraha alighted at al-Mughammas, he sent a man of the Abyssinians called al-Aswad ibn Maqsud [so in some copies of the original and in Tafsir al-Tha'labi, Tarikh al-Tabari (first part, p.937, European edition) and Tarikh Ibn al-Athir (vol.1, p.321, European edition). In some copies: Tafsir al-Tabari and Sira of Ibn Hisham (p.33, European edition): "Mafsud" with fa' instead of qaf] on his horses. He reached Mecca and drove off to him the property of the people of Tihama from Quraysh and others, and he seized two hundred camels belonging to 'Abd al-Muttalib ibn Hashim, who was then the greatest and chief of Quraysh. Quraysh, Kinana, Hudhayl and those who were in that sanctuary resolved to fight him, but then they knew they had no power against him, so they abandoned that. Abraha sent Hunata al-Himyari to Mecca and said to him: "Ask about the lord of this town [in a margin of one copy: 'about the lord of this House'] and its chief, then say to him: 'The king says: I have not come to fight you. I have come only to demolish this House. If you do not confront me with war, I have no need of your blood. If he does not intend to fight me, bring him to me.'" When Hunata entered Mecca, he asked about the lord and chief of Quraysh, and he was told: "'Abd al-Muttalib ibn Hashim." He came to him and said what Abraha had instructed him. 'Abd al-Muttalib said to him: "By Allah, we do not intend to fight him, and we have no power for that against him. This is the Sacred House of Allah and the house of His friend Ibrahim, peace be upon him, or as he said. If He protects it from him, it is His sanctuary and His house; and if He leaves him to it, by Allah, we have no defence of it." Hunata said to him: "Then go to him, for he has ordered me to bring you to him." So 'Abd al-Muttalib went with him, and with him some of his sons, until they came to the army. He asked about Dhu Nafr, who was his friend, until he entered upon him while he was in his prison. He said to him: "O Dhu Nafr, do you have any help in what has befallen us?" Dhu Nafr said: "What help can a captive in the hands of a king have, who awaits being killed morning and evening? I have no help in anything that has befallen you, except that Unays, the elephant-keeper, is my friend. I will send to him and recommend you to him, and I will impress upon him your rights, and ask him to seek permission for you from the king, so you may speak to him as you wish, and he may intercede for you with him for good, if he is able to do so." 'Abd al-Muttalib said: "That is sufficient for me." Dhu Nafr sent to Unays and said to him: "'Abd al-Muttalib is the lord of Quraysh and the owner of the spring of Mecca. He feeds the people in the plain and the wild beasts on the mountain tops. The king has seized two hundred camels of his. So seek permission for him to see him, and help him with him as far as you can." He said: "I will do so." Unays spoke to Abraha and said: "O king, this is the lord of Quraysh at your gate, seeking to be admitted to you. He is the owner of the spring of Mecca, who feeds the people in the plain and the wild beasts on the mountain tops. So admit him to you, so that he may speak to you about his need." He said: So Abraha admitted him. 'Abd al-Muttalib was the most handsome, the greatest and the most beautiful of people. When Abraha saw him, he esteemed him highly and greatly, so that he would not seat him beneath himself. Abraha got down from his throne and sat on his carpet and seated him with him beside him. Then he said to his interpreter: "Say to him: What is your need?" The interpreter said that to him, and he said: "My need is that the king return to me the two hundred camels he took from me." When he said that, Abraha said to his interpreter: "Tell him: I was impressed by you when I saw you, but now I have lost interest in you since you spoke to me. Do you speak to me about two hundred camels I have taken from you, and leave a House which is your religion and the religion of your fathers, which I have come to demolish? Do not speak to me about it!" 'Abd al-Muttalib said to him: "I am the lord of the camels, and the House has a Lord who will protect it." He said: "It could not resist me!" He said: "You and that." So he returned his camels to him. 'Abd al-Muttalib went back to Quraysh and informed them of the news, and ordered them to leave Mecca and take refuge on the peaks of the mountains and in the ravines, fearing for them the harm of the army [*al-mu'arra*: harm. The harm of an army is that it alights among a people and eats their crops without their permission. It is also said: their trampling of whoever they pass by, whether Muslim or protected, and their striking of them in their sanctuaries, property and crops, in ways not permitted to them]. Then 'Abd al-Muttalib stood, took hold of the ring of the door of the Ka'ba, and a group of Quraysh stood with him, calling upon Allah and seeking His help against Abraha and his army. 'Abd al-Muttalib, while holding the ring of the door of the Ka'ba, said:

*O Allah, indeed a servant defends his camp,*
*so defend Your inhabitants.*
*Let not their cross and their might prevail*
*against Your might, by their aggression.*
*If they enter the sacred town*
*then do what seems right to You.*

He means: whatever seems right to You, which You have never done to us before. *Al-hilal* is the plural of *hill*, meaning those who dwell permanently and are neighbours; they are the inhabitants of the sanctuary. *Al-mihal* means strength. It is also said that when 'Abd al-Muttalib took hold of the ring of the door of the Ka'ba he said:

*O Lord, I hope for no one but You for them.*
*O Lord, defend from them Your sanctuary.*
*Indeed the enemy of the House is whoever opposes You.*
*They will never overpower Your strength.*

'Ikrima ibn 'Amir ibn Hashim ibn 'Abd Manaf ibn 'Abd al-Dar ibn Qusayy said:

*O Allah, disgrace al-Aswad ibn Maqsud,*
*who seized the herd, in which is the garland of identification* [*al-hajma*: a large portion of camels. It is said it is between thirty and a hundred; it is also said its beginning is forty, and it is also said between seventy and a hundred (see the lexicons). Its garlanding means that a token was placed on its neck so that it would be known as an offering.]
*between Hira and Thabir and the deserts,*
*holding them back, while they are driven in succession.*
*He gathered them with black barbarians*
*who have agreed that no one should be worshipped* [al-Suhayli: "black barbarians" means the uncivilised ones.]
*and who will demolish the sacred House, the pillared one,*
*and the two Marwas and the dark sacred sites.* [What is between the brackets was not mentioned by Ibn Ishaq in his transmission.]
*Betray him, O Lord, for You are praised.* [*Akhfarahu*: break his covenant and his resolve so that You do not grant him security.]

Ibn Ishaq said: Then 'Abd al-Muttalib let go of the ring of the door of the Ka'bah, and he and those of Quraysh with him set off for the mountain peaks, where they took cover, waiting to see what Abraha would do to Makkah when he entered it.

When morning came, Abraha prepared to enter Makkah. He readied his elephant and arranged his army. The elephant's name was Mahmud, and Abraha was determined to demolish the House and then return to Yemen. When they turned the elephant toward Makkah, Nufayl ibn Habib came forward, stood beside the elephant, took hold of its ear, and said: "Kneel down, Mahmud, and go back safely the way you came, for you are in the sacred land of Allah." He then released its ear, and the elephant knelt down. Nufayl ibn Habib ran off and climbed up the mountain.

They struck the elephant to make it stand, but it refused. They struck it on the head with the tabarzin [[The tabar (with a vowel on the first letter): an axe, an arabized weapon. The tabarzin is a weapon resembling the tabar. It is said it is the same as the tabar.]] to make it stand, but it refused. They then inserted their hooked staffs [[The mihjan: a staff with a curved head, like a mace.]] into its flanks and goaded it with them [[Bazaghu: pierced it / goaded it.]] to make it stand, but it refused. They turned it back toward Yemen, and it rose and ran at a trot. They turned it toward Syria, and it did the same. They turned it toward the east, and it did the same. Then they turned it toward Makkah, and it knelt down.

Allah sent against them birds from the sea, like the khatatif [swallows] and the balasan [[In al-Lisan and al-Nihayah, under the root b-l-s: "'Abbad ibn Musa said: I think they were the zarazir (starlings)."]]. Each bird carried three stones: one in its beak and two in its feet, the size of chickpeas and lentils. Whoever was struck by one was destroyed, though not all of them were struck. They fled in panic along the road by which they had come, asking about Nufayl ibn Habib so that he might guide them to the road to Yemen. When Nufayl ibn Habib saw the vengeance Allah had brought upon them, he said:

"Where is the escape, when the Seeking God is the Pursuer?
The Broken-Nosed, the Defeated, is not the Victor."

He also said:

"I praised Allah when I saw the birds,
and I feared the stones that would be hurled upon us.
All the people ask about Nufayl,
as though I owed the Abyssinians a debt."

They went out falling down along every road and perishing at every place of descent [[In Ibn Hisham's Sirah: "every watering place"]]. Abraha was struck in his body, and they carried him with them while his body was falling apart, one joint at a time. Whenever a joint fell from him, pus and blood flowed out after it, until they brought him to Sana'a, where he was like a young bird. He did not die until his chest split open and his heart came out, so they claim.

Al-Kalbi and Muqatil ibn Sulayman (one of them adds to this account and the other omits) said: The cause of the Elephant event is what is related: some young men of Quraysh set out as merchants to the land of the Negus. They stopped on the seashore by a church of the Christians, which the Christians call the Haykal. They lit a fire to cook their food, then left it and departed. A violent wind blew onto the fire, which set the church ablaze, and it burned down. A messenger came to the Negus and informed him, and he flew into a rage. Abraha ibn al-Sabbah, Hujr ibn Shurahbil and Abu Yaksum al-Kindiyyun came to him and guaranteed that they would burn the Ka'bah and take Makkah captive. The Negus was the king, Abraha was the commander of the army, Abu Yaksum was the king's boon companion, and it is said he was his vizier, and Hujr ibn Shurahbil was one of his commanders. Mujahid said: Abu Yaksum was Abraha ibn al-Sabbah.

They marched, and the elephant was with them. Most scholars say it was a single elephant. Al-Dahhak said there were eight elephants. They camped at Dhu al-Majaz and seized the herds of Makkah, among which were the camels of 'Abd al-Muttalib. A herdsman came as a warner, climbed to al-Safa, and shouted: "Waṣabahah!" Then he informed the people of the arrival of the army and the elephant. 'Abd al-Muttalib went out, made his way to Abraha, and asked him for his camels.

There is disagreement about whether the Negus was with them. Some said he was, but most said he was not.

The people of Makkah looked at the birds that had come from the direction of the sea. 'Abd al-Muttalib said: "These birds are strangers in our land. They are neither from Najd, nor Tihamah, nor the Hijaz, and they resemble the yaʿasib [the leader of the bees]. There were stones in their beaks and feet. When they appeared [in another version: came] over the people, they dropped them on them until they perished." 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah said: The birds came in the evening, spent the night, and then at dawn attacked them and pelted them. Al-Kalbi said: In their beaks were pebbles like the pebbles of khadhf [[Khadhf: throwing small pebbles with the fingertips.]], and in front of each flock was a bird leading it, red-beaked, black-headed, and long-necked. When they came to the army's encampment and gathered, they poured what was in their beaks upon those below them, and on each stone was written the name of the one it would kill. It is said that on each stone was written: "Whoever obeys Allah is saved, and whoever disobeys Him goes astray." Then they wheeled away, returning the way they had come. Al-Awfi said: I asked Abu Sa'id al-Khudri about them, and he said: "They are among the pigeons of Makkah." It is also said that a stone would fall on one of them's helmet [[That is, the iron helmet.]], pierce it, enter his brain, and pass through the elephant and the animal. The stone would sink into the earth from the force of its impact.

The companions of the elephant numbered sixty thousand, and none of them returned except their commander, who went back with a small remnant. When they reported what they had seen, they perished.

Al-Waqidi said: Abraha was the grandfather of the Negus who was in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Abraha was known as al-Ashram, and he was given this name because he had a dispute [[Al-Mufatanah: people disagreeing over opinions and the fighting that occurs between them.]] with Ariyat, until they clashed in battle. Then they agreed to meet in single combat, and whoever won would have authority. They fought each other. Ariyat was a huge, great man, with a spear in his hand, while Abraha was short, stocky [[Al-hadir: well-built in physique.]], forbearing, and devout in Christianity. Abraha had a vizier called 'Atwadah. When they drew near, Ariyat struck Abraha's head with his spear, and it fell on his forehead, slashing his eye, nose, forehead, and lip, which is why he was named al-Ashram. 'Atwadah charged at Ariyat and killed him. The Abyssinians rallied to Abraha, and the Negus became angry and swore that he would shave Abraha's forelock and trample his land. Abraha shaved his forelock, filled a pouch with dirt from his land, and sent both to the Negus, saying: "I was only your slave, and I am your slave. I am in charge of the Abyssinian affairs, and I have shaved my forelock and sent you dirt from my land so that you may trample it and fulfil your oath." The Negus was pleased with him. Then Abraha built a church in Sana'a to divert the pilgrimage of the Arabs toward it, as has been mentioned before.

Fourth: Muqatil said: The Year of the Elephant was forty years before the birth of the Prophet (ﷺ). Al-Kalbi and 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr said: It was twenty-three years before the birth of the Prophet (ﷺ). The sound report is what was related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "I was born in the Year of the Elephant." It is also related from him that he said: "On the Day of the Elephant." Al-Mawardi recounted this in his tafsir [[Tafsir: Qur'anic exegesis.]]. In his book A'lam al-Nubuwwah, he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was born on Monday, the twelfth of Rabi' al-Awwal, fifty days after the Elephant, and it coincided with the twentieth of Asbat in the Roman months, in the twelfth year of the reign of Hormuz ibn Anushirwan. He said: Abu Ja'far al-Tabari related that the birth of the Prophet (ﷺ) was in the forty-second year of the reign of Anushirwan. It has also been said: his mother Aminah conceived him on the day of 'Ashura' in Muharram, and he was born on Monday, twelve nights into Ramadan, so the period of his pregnancy was eight full months and two days of the ninth. It has also been said that he was born on the day of 'Ashura' in the month of Muharram, as related by Ibn Shahin [[In some copies of the original: "Abu Shahin Hafs."]] Abu Hafs, in his book on the virtues of the day of 'Ashura'.

Ibn al-'Arabi said: "Ibn Wahb related from Malik: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was born in the Year of the Elephant. Qays ibn Makhramah said: I and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) were born in the Year of the Elephant. People have related from Malik that he said: 'Part of a man's manliness is that he does not disclose his age, for if he is young they will belittle him, and if he is old they will call him decrepit.' This is a weak statement, for Malik did not disclose the age of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and kept his age hidden, though he is one of the greatest scholars to be emulated. There is nothing wrong with a man disclosing his age, whether he is old or young."

'Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan said to 'Attab ibn Asid: "Are you older, or the Prophet (ﷺ)?" He said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) is older than me, and I am older than him. The Prophet (ﷺ) was born in the Year of the Elephant, and I met his groomsman and his guide, both blind and crippled, begging from the people." It was said to one of the judges: "How old are you?" He said: "The age of 'Attab ibn Asid when the Prophet (ﷺ) appointed him over Makkah," and at that time he was under twenty.

Fifth: Our scholars said: The story of the Elephant, though it occurred before the Prophet's time and before the challenge, was among the miracles of the Prophet (ﷺ) that came later, because it was a confirmation of his affair and a preparation for his station. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited this surah to them, there were many in Makkah who had witnessed that event, and that is why He said: ﴿Have you not seen?﴾. There was no one in Makkah who had not seen the leader and driver of the elephant, both blind, begging from the people. 'Aishah, may Allah be pleased with her, said, despite her young age: "I saw the leader and driver of the elephant, both blind, begging from the people." Abu Salih said: "In the house of Umm Hani' bint Abi Talib I saw about two qafizes [[A qafiz: a measure of volume.]] of those stones, black and streaked with red."

﴿Did He not make their plot go astray?﴾ That is, He made it futile and lost, because they intended to wreak havoc on Quraysh by killing and taking captives, and to destroy and demolish the House (the Ka'bah).

It is related about ʿAbd al-Muttalib that he sent his son ʿAbdullah on his horse to look at what the people had met from those birds. He found the people all crushed together, so he returned galloping his horse and uncovering his thigh. When his father saw this, he said: "My son is the most horseman-like of the Arabs." He had uncovered his thigh only as a bearer of good news or a warner. When he drew near to their gathering place, within earshot of them, they said: "What is behind you?" He said: "They have all perished." So ʿAbd al-Muttalib and his companions went out and took their property. The wealth of the sons of ʿAbd al-Muttalib came from that, and through it ʿAbd al-Muttalib's leadership was completed, for he carried off whatever he wished of gold and silver. Then the people of Mecca went out after him and plundered.

It was also said that ʿAbd al-Muttalib dug two pits, filled them with gold and jewels, and then said to Abu Masʿud al-Thaqafi, who was a close friend of ʿAbd al-Muttalib: "Choose whichever of them you want." Then the people took of their wealth until they were exhausted. At that, ʿAbd al-Muttalib said:

You prevented the Abyssinians and the elephants,
and they had pastured on the mountains of Mecca.

We feared fighting from them,
and every affair of theirs was a grave difficulty.

Thanks and praise to You, O Possessor of Majesty.

Ibn Ishaq said: When God turned the Abyssinians away from Mecca, the Arabs magnified Quraysh and said: "They are the people of God; God fought on their behalf and sufficed them against their enemy." ʿAbdullah ibn ʿAmr ibn Makhzum, in the story of the People of the Elephant, said:

You are the Majestic, our Lord, who is never defiled.
You held back the elephant at al-Mughammis,
after it had intended evil, despairing.
You held it in the state of one overturned,
and for them there is no relief nor respite.

Al-mukarkas: the overturned, cast down.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: They were birds from the sky, of a kind never seen before or after them.

Juwaybir narrated from al-Dahhak, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "They are birds between the sky and the earth, that nest and hatch."

From Ibn 'Abbas: they had beaks like the beaks of birds, and palms like the palms of dogs.

'Ikrimah said: They were green birds that came out of the sea, with heads like the heads of beasts of prey, and nothing like them was seen before or after.

'A'isha (may Allah be pleased with her) said: They were most similar to al-khatatif (swallows).

It was also said: Rather, they resembled al-watawit (bats), red and black.

Also from Sa'id ibn Jubayr: They are green birds with yellow beaks. It was also said: they were white.

Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: They are black sea birds, with stones in their beaks and talons.

It was also said: They are al-'anqa' al-mughrib (the phoenix-like bird) [[She is the one that went far off in the lands, so she became remote, was not sensed, and was not seen.]], which proverbs are coined about.

'Ikrimah said: Ababil means "gathered together" (mujtama'ah).

It was said: "following one another," one after another, as stated by Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid.

It was said: "varied and scattered," coming from every direction, from here and there, as stated by Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Zayd and al-Akhfash.

Al-Nahhas said: These statements agree, and the true meaning is that they were great groups. It is said: "Fulan yu'abbilu 'ala Fulan," meaning he grows great over him and increases against him, and this is derived from al-ibil (camels).

Scholars differed about the singular of (ababil). Al-Jawhari said: Al-Akhfash said: it is said, "Your camels came ababil," meaning in separate groups, and "birds ababil." He said: This comes in the sense of abundance, and it is from the plural that has no singular (jam' la wahida lahu, a collective plural with no singular form). Some of them said: its singular is ibbawl, like 'ijjawl. Some said, and he is al-Mubarrad: ibbil, like sikkin (knife). He said: I have not found the Arabs knowing a singular for it except in the (reliable) authorities. It was also said that its singular is ibbal.

Ru'ba ibn al-'Ajjaj said, using it as a plural:

"And birds played with them in ababil,
so they became like chewed-up straw."

Al-A'sha said:

"A road and a jabbar [[al-jabbar among palms: what grows tall and beyond the reach of the hand.]] lush at its roots,
upon it are ababil of birds, calling out."

Another said:

"My mount was almost shattered by the sounds,
when the earth flowed with the al-jurd [[al-jurd (with a dammah, like al-jaridah): horses without foot soldiers among them. Al-jurd also means short hair on the hide of a horse, which is one of the praised descriptions of horses.]] al-ababil."

Another said:

"You see them rushing to the caller like
ababil of birds under a dark, dense cloud."

[[So it is in the copies of the original text (with a dotted kha' and nun). In Tafsir al-Tha'labi: ... tahta dajin musahhar (with an undotted ha' and ra'). He attributed it to Imru' al-Qays, but we did not find it in his diwan. Perhaps the correct reading is: ... tahta dajin musakhkhar (with a dotted kha' and ra').]]

Al-Farra' said: It has no singular from its own form. Al-Ru'asi, who was trustworthy, claimed that he heard its singular as "ibbalah" with a shadda. Al-Farra' also related "ibalah" without a shadda. He said: I heard some Arabs say: "dighth 'ala ibalah," meaning abundance upon abundance. He said: If someone said "ibal," it would be correct, like dinar and dananiyr. Ishaq ibn 'Abd Allah ibn al-Harith ibn Nawfal said: Ababil is derived from al-ibil al-mu'abbalah, which are the herds (al-aqatee').

In al-Sihah: "with stones of sijjil." They said: "They are stones of clay, baked in the fire of Hell, on which the names of the people are written, in accordance with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That We may send down upon them stones of clay, marked by your Lord﴾ [adh-Dhariyat 51:33-34]."[[Verse 33 of Surat adh-Dhariyat.]]

'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abza said: "'From sijjil' means from the sky, and these are the stones that descended upon the people of Lut." It was also said: "From al-Jahim." And it is "sijjin" (from sijjin), with the lam changed to a nun, just as they said Usaylan for Usaylal. Ibn Muqbil said:

"Striking blows that the heroes had agreed upon, sijjina."[[The first half of the verse as it appears in Lisan al-'Arab: "And a brave company striking the white swords from the side."]]

But the original is sijjil. Al-Zajjaj said: "'Min sijjil' means: of that which was written for them to be punished with, derived from al-sijill (the register)." The discussion of sijjil has already been given in full in Surat Hud.[[See vol. 9, p. 81.]]

'Ikrima said: "They would strike them with stones that were with them, and whoever was struck by one of these stones would break out in smallpox, which had not been seen before that day. The stone was the size of a chickpea and larger than a lentil." Ibn 'Abbas said: "When a stone fell upon one of them, his skin would blister, and that was the first smallpox."

The recitation of the common readers is "tarmihim" with the ta', because the group of birds is feminine. Al-A'raj and Talha read "yarmihim" with the ya', meaning: Allah strikes them. Its evidence is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But it was Allah who threw﴾ [al-Anfal 8:17].[[Verse 17 of Surat al-Anfal.]] It is also permissible that it refers back to the birds, since they lack feminine markers and their femininity is not real (haqiqi).

So He made them like eaten straw (5). That is, Allah made the companions of the Elephant like the leaves of a crop when beasts have eaten it and cast it out from below. He likened the dismemberment of their limbs to the scattering of its parts. This meaning is reported from Ibn Zayd and others. The discussion of "al-'asf" (chaff, straw) has already been given in the commentary on Surat al-Rahman [[See vol. 17, p. 156.]]. Among the things that show it means the leaves of a crop is the verse of Alqamah:

They water channels whose chaff has bent over, its lower parts drenched by the flowing water [[Al-madhanib: water channels. Al-'asifah: the gathered leaves in which the ear of grain is found. Hudurha: what has run down from it and settled. Al-ati (like ghani): the stream. Al-matmum: filled with water.]].

Ru'bah ibn al-Ajjaj said:

Such befell them as befell the companions of the Elephant,
Stones of sijjil [baked clay] pelting them,
And birds played over them in flocks,
So they became like eaten straw.

Al-'asf is a plural; its singular is 'asfah, 'usafah, and 'asifah. He introduced the particle "ka" (like) in "ka'asfin" for comparison, together with "mithl" (like), as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿There is nothing like unto Him﴾ [Al-Shura: 11]. The meaning of "ma'kul" is "ma'kul" (eaten), its grain having been eaten. It is like saying "Fulan is handsome," meaning his face is handsome.

Ibn Abbas said regarding "So He made them like eaten straw" that what is meant is the husk of wheat, that is, the covering in which the wheat grain is found. It is related that the stone would fall upon one of them and bring out everything in his interior, so he would remain like the husk of wheat after the grain has come out of it. Ibn Mas'ud said: When the birds threw the stones, Allah sent a wind which struck the stones and increased their force, so that they did not fall on anyone without destroying him, and none of them was saved except a man from Kindah [[He was Nufayl ibn Habib, as in the History of al-Tabari and Ibn al-Athir.]], who said:

If you had seen, though you did not see it,
At the side of al-Mughammas what we saw...

[[In the manuscripts of the original: "wa law taranā" (and if you had seen us), which is an error, since he is addressing a woman. The verses as cited by al-Tabari (p. 942, first part, European edition) and Ibn al-Athir (vol. 1, p. 322, European edition):

Ah, may you be greeted, O Rudayna, from us; we greeted you with eyes at dawn.
A rider of yours came to us at evening, but he did not reach our rider at our place.
Rudayna, had you seen, but you did not see it, at the side of al-Muhassab what we saw,
Then you would have excused me and praised my opinion, and you would not grieve over what has passed.
I praised Allah when I saw birds, and I feared stones that would fall upon us.
For all the people ask about Nufayl, as if I owed the Abyssinians a debt.]]

I feared Allah when He scattered birds
And a cloud's shadow passed over us.
All of them began calling out with the truth,
As if they had a debt owed to the Abyssinians.

It is also reported that it did not strike all of them, but struck whomever Allah willed among them. It has already been mentioned that their commander returned, and a small remnant was with him; when they told of what they had seen, they perished. And Allah knows best.

Ibn Ishaq said: When Allah turned back the Abyssinians from Makkah, the Arabs exalted Quraysh and said: "They are the people of Allah; He fought on their behalf and spared them the burden of their enemy." That was a blessing from Allah upon them.
